entry: German invasion of [[Belgium]], Luxembourg, the Netherlands and France, May 10–June 25, 1940, during the [[World War II|Second World War]]. German armoured units advanced through the Ardennes and cut off Allied forces that had entered Belgium; British and French navies evacuated encircled troops from Dunkirk. Germany occupied Paris unopposed on June 14. Under the armistice of June 22, 1940, the Vichy regime led by [[Philippe Pétain|Marshal Philippe Pétain]] governed the south, while German forces occupied the Atlantic and North Sea coasts.

[[American Civil War]] clash near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, July 1–3, 1863. Union forces under George Meade defeated attacks by [[Robert E. Lee]]'s Army of Northern Virginia, halting Lee's invasion of the North and forcing his retreat. It is widely considered the turning point of the war, leading to the preservation of the Union and freedom from slavery. Between 46,000 and 51,000 soldiers from both armies were casualties, the most in any battle in American history up to that time. [[Abraham Lincoln|Lincoln]] spoke at the dedication of Gettysburg National Cemetery on November 19, delivering his 271-word [[Gettysburg Address]].

Norman victory over English forces under King Harold Godwinson, October 14, 1066, near Hastings in present-day East Sussex, England. It began the [[Norman Conquest]] of England. Harold had been forced to march south swiftly after his victory at [[Battle of Stamford Bridge|Stamford Bridge]], and William landed at Pevensey on September 28. Harold was probably killed near the end of the battle, after which most of his army retreated. William was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066.

Amphibious assault on Japanese-held Iwo Jima, February 19–March 26, 1945, in the [[World War II|Second World War]]. [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]], Navy and Army units captured the island from the Imperial Japanese Army, including its two airfields. Of 21,000 Japanese soldiers on the island at the start, only 216 were taken prisoner. American casualties exceeded Japanese casualties, at three for every two. Joe Rosenthal's [[Associated Press]] photograph of the flag raised on Mount Suribachi became a famous image of the battle.

Naval battle of the First World War, May 31–June 1, 1916, off the [[North Sea]] coast of Denmark's Jutland Peninsula. Britain's [[Royal Navy]] Grand Fleet under Admiral Sir John Jellicoe fought Germany's High Seas Fleet under Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer. It was the largest naval battle and the only full-scale clash of battleships in the war. Fourteen British and eleven German ships sank, with 9,823 casualties. Both sides claimed victory. The British kept the German fleet contained, and the battle reinforced German avoidance of all fleet-to-fleet contact.

Eastern Front battle of the [[World War II|Second World War]], summer 1943, near Kursk in southwestern Russia. Germany's Operation Citadel, begun on July 5 to pinch off the Kursk salient, stalled against Soviet defences in depth, and [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] cancelled it after about a week, in part to divert forces to Italy. It was Germany's final strategic offensive on the Eastern Front, and its heavy losses left the [[Red Army]] with the strategic initiative for the rest of the war.

Coalition victory over Napoleon's *Grande Armée* near Leipzig, Saxony, October 16–19, 1813. Armies of Austria, Prussia, Sweden and Russia, led by [[Alexander I of Russia|Tsar Alexander I]] and Karl von Schwarzenberg, defeated the French. The battle involved about 560,000 soldiers, 2,200 artillery pieces and 133,000 casualties. Also called the Battle of the Nations, it was the largest of the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and arguably the deciding battle of the wars. Napoleon was compelled to return to France and was exiled to Elba in May 1814 after abdicating.

Naval battle of the [[World War II|Second World War]], October 23–26, 1944, in waters around Leyte Island in the [[Philippines]]. It was the largest naval battle of the war and, by some criteria, in history, with over 200,000 naval personnel involved. The Imperial Japanese Navy mobilized nearly all its remaining major vessels to contest the Allied invasion of the Philippines, but was defeated by the U.S. Third and Seventh Fleets. It was the first battle in which Japanese aircraft carried out organized kamikaze attacks.

Greek victory over a Persian invasion force in 490 BC, on the plain of Marathon in Attica. The Persian expedition, sent by King Darius I to punish [[Athens]] and Eretria for supporting the Ionian Revolt, landed at Marathon. An Athenian army of about 10,000 hoplites, reinforced by around 1,000 Plataeans, blocked the exits of the plain. The [[Sparta|Spartans]], asked for help, did not come, citing a religious festival. Miltiades reinforced his flanks, and the wheeling flanks enveloped the Persians, who broke and fled toward their ships. According to [[Herodotus]], 6,400 Persians and 192 Greeks died, though modern analyses adjust these figures downward. The victory ended the first Persian invasion of Greece and is often seen as a turning point in the [[Greco-Persian Wars]]. [[Xerxes I]] launched a second invasion in 480 BC.

Naval battle of the [[Pacific War]], June 4–7, 1942, near [[Midway Atoll]] in the central Pacific. The Japanese Combined Fleet under [[Isoroku Yamamoto]] sought to capture Midway and draw out the U.S. Pacific Fleet's carriers, but U.S. codebreakers had determined the date and location of the attack. Carrier aircraft struck Chuichi Nagumo's force while its carriers were rearming and refueling, sinking all four Japanese fleet carriers present. Japan also lost 3,000 men, and the U.S. lost the carrier Yorktown. With the [[Guadalcanal campaign]], the battle is widely considered a turning point in the Pacific War.

Clash in Mogadishu, Somalia, October 3–4, 1993, between US forces and Somali National Alliance fighters. Also called the Black Hawk Down incident, it was part of Operation Gothic Serpent, a raid to seize two lieutenants of General Mohammed Farah Aidid during the [[Somali Civil War]]. Somali insurgents shot down three American Black Hawk helicopters with rocket-propelled grenades, turning the raid into an overnight battle. 18 American soldiers were killed and 73 wounded. Somali casualties, including civilians, are estimated at 133 to 700 dead. All [[United Nations|UN]] forces had withdrawn from Somalia by early 1995.

[[Pacific War]] battle, April 1–June 22, 1945, on Okinawa in the [[Ryukyu Islands]]. Codenamed Operation Iceberg, it was fought by US Army and [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] forces against the Japanese Thirty-Second Army under Mitsuru Ushijima. The initial landing on April 1 was the largest amphibious assault in the Pacific Theater of World War II. The Allies planned to use Kadena Air Base as a staging point for the invasion of the Japanese home islands. Casualties were some 50,000 Allied and around 100,000 Japanese. According to local authorities, at least 149,425 Okinawans were killed, died by coerced suicide or went missing.

Allied campaign of the First World War, July–November 1917, for ridges near Ypres in [[Flanders]], Belgium. Also called the Third Battle of Ypres, it was fought by the Allies against the [[German Empire]] for ridges south and east of Ypres, part of a strategy to advance toward [[Bruges]] and the Belgian coast. Unusually wet weather and autumn rains hampered the advance. The Canadian Corps captured Passchendaele in November. The campaign was controversial in 1917, and Prime Minister [[David Lloyd George]] opposed the offensive.

Engagement in what is now Gifu Prefecture, Japan, October 21, 1600, at the end of the [[Sengoku period]]. Forces of [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] defeated a coalition loyal to the Toyotomi clan, led by Ishida Mitsunari on behalf of the young Toyotomi Hideyori, after several commanders defected. It is often regarded as the most important battle in Japanese history. Mitsunari's defeat is generally considered the beginning of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]], which ruled Japan for two and a half centuries until 1868.

Urban battle of the [[World War II|Second World War]] on the Eastern Front, from late August 1942 to February 2, 1943, for the industrial city of Stalingrad (now Volgograd) on the Volga River. [[Nazi Germany]] and its Axis allies fought the [[Soviet Union]], and the battle is considered the largest and deadliest urban battle in military history. The German 6th Army advanced into a city reduced to rubble by air raids and fought house to house. On November 19 the [[Red Army]] launched Operation Uranus and encircled the 6th Army. Hitler forbade a breakout, and the army surrendered on February 2, 1943, the first of Hitler's field armies to do so. The Soviet victory is generally regarded as a turning point of the European theatre of the war.

English victory over a Norwegian invasion force led by Harald Hardrada, at Stamford Bridge, East Riding of Yorkshire, September 25, 1066. Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson, brother of the English king, were killed along with most of the Norwegians. King Harold's army was defeated by the [[Normans]] at [[Battle of Hastings|Hastings]] less than three weeks later. The battle is traditionally presented as marking the end of the [[Viking Age]], although Scandinavian campaigns in Britain and Ireland continued in the following decades.

Engagement of the second Persian invasion of [[Greece]] in 480 BC, at a narrow pass in central Greece. A Greek force of about 7,000 men, including an estimated 300 Spartans, under [[Leonidas I]] held the pass against the army of [[Xerxes I]] for seven days, including three of direct battle. A local resident, Ephialtes, revealed a path behind the Greek lines. Leonidas dismissed most of the army and remained with a rearguard, which was annihilated. Modern scholars estimate the Persian army at 120,000 to 300,000 soldiers.

Naval battle of the [[Napoleonic Wars]], October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar, Spain. A [[Royal Navy]] fleet under [[Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson|Horatio Nelson]] attacked a combined French and Spanish fleet under Pierre-Charles Villeneuve in two columns, splitting it into three groups. The British captured or destroyed 18 French and Spanish ships and lost none. Nelson was shot by a French marksman and died before the battle ended. The victory confirmed British naval supremacy and ended any real French effort to invade Britain.

Longest battle of the First World War, February 21–December 18, 1916, on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] in France. The German 5th Army attacked the Fortified Region of Verdun, hoping to capture the Meuse Heights and force the French to commit their reserves. [[Philippe Pétain]] ordered that there be no retreat. The Germans captured Fort Douaumont four days after the attack began and came within 2.5 miles (4 km) of the Verdun citadel. In 2000, Hannes Heer and Klaus Naumann calculated 714,231 casualties, 377,231 of them French and 337,000 German. The battle lasted 302 days.

Engagement on Kahlenberg Mountain near [[Vienna]] on September 12, 1683, after a two-month [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] siege of the city. A coalition of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], led by King John III Sobieski of Poland, defeated an Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha. The Lithuanian army arrived only after the city had been relieved. Some historians regard the battle as a turning point in the Ottoman–Habsburg wars, a 300-year struggle between the Holy Roman and Ottoman empires. In the war that followed, lasting until 1699, most of Ottoman Hungary was ceded to [[Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor|Leopold I]]. The battle is noted for including the largest known cavalry charge in history.

[[Napoleon]]'s final engagement, June 18, 1815, near Waterloo in present-day [[Belgium]]. An Anglo-allied army under the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Gebhard von Blücher defeated the French army. Prussian troops attacked the French flank, and the Imperial Guard's final assault was repulsed. Napoleon abdicated four days later, ending the [[Hundred Days]]. It was the second-bloodiest single-day battle of the Napoleonic Wars, after Borodino.

Siege and assault in the Texas Revolution, February 23–March 6, 1836, at the Alamo Mission near [[San Antonio]]. About one hundred Texians were garrisoned at the mission and joined by around one hundred reinforcements, under James Bowie and William B. Travis. After a 13-day siege, Mexican troops under [[Antonio López de Santa Anna|Santa Anna]] attacked on March 6, and nearly all Texian combatants were killed. Santa Anna's execution of surrendering soldiers inspired many Texians to join the army, which defeated his forces at San Jacinto on April 21, 1836.

Naval campaign of the [[World War II|Second World War]], from 1939 to Germany's defeat in May 1945, and the longest continuous military campaign of the war. It pitted German [[U-boat|U-boats]], other warships and Luftwaffe aircraft against the [[Royal Navy]], the Royal Canadian Navy and the United States Navy, which protected Allied merchant convoys. Britain needed more than a million tons of imported material each week, making the campaign a tonnage war. Some 3,500 merchant ships and 175 warships were sunk, for the loss of 783 U-boats and 47 German surface warships. The Allies gradually gained the upper hand, overcoming German surface raiders by the end of 1942 and defeating the U-boats by mid-1943. [[Winston Churchill]] wrote, "The only thing that really frightened me during the war was the U-boat peril."

German offensive through the Ardennes region of eastern [[Belgium]] and northern [[Luxembourg]], December 16, 1944–January 25, 1945. Also called the Ardennes Offensive, it aimed to stop Allied use of the port of [[Antwerp]] and split the Allied lines. The Germans achieved total surprise, but American resistance at Bastogne blocked key roads until [[George S. Patton|General George S. Patton]]'s Third Army reached the town from the south on December 26. Between 63,000 and 104,000 German men were killed, missing, wounded or captured. It was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the Second World War.

Armed engagement of the Great Sioux War, June 25–26, 1876, along the Little Bighorn River in southeastern [[Montana]] Territory. Known to the Lakota as the Battle of the Greasy Grass, and in popular memory as Custer's Last Stand, it pitted Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho forces against the 7th Cavalry Regiment of the United States Army under Lieutenant Colonel [[George Armstrong Custer]]. Custer was killed, and five of the regiment's twelve troops were wiped out. U.S. casualties totaled 268 dead and 55 severely wounded.
